**Somebody Decided**

The yellow light lasts about four seconds, and it lasts that long on purpose.

In 1960, three physicists at General Motors' research labs, Gazis, Herman, and Maradudin, published a paper on what they called the problem of the amber signal light. They had noticed that at some intersections there was a stretch of road where a driver, at the moment the light changed, was too close to stop comfortably and too far away to clear the intersection in time. The fix was arithmetic: a reaction time, plus speed divided by twice a tolerable deceleration. Traffic engineers still use a descendant of that equation. So whenever you've rolled through a yellow and felt you judged it well, part of the judging was done for you decades earlier, by someone who assumed you'd need about a second to notice.

I keep coming back to how much of the world is like this. I don't mean designed in the grand sense, like cathedrals and suspension bridges. I mean decided: a number chosen by someone, poured into concrete, and forgotten.

Take stairs. American building codes say the risers in a single flight can differ from each other by no more than three-eighths of an inch. That sounds fussy until you learn that your legs memorize a staircase within two or three steps and stop consulting your eyes. In 2012 a filmmaker pointed a camera at a subway stairway in Brooklyn where one step was a fraction taller than the others. He recorded person after person stumbling at the same spot, each presumably blaming their own feet. The step was fixed soon after. For years it had been tripping people who each thought they were alone.

Or the dial tone. In North America it was two pitches sounded together, 350 and 440 hertz, roughly an F and an A. For decades a continent picked up the phone and heard the same major third, and almost no one could have told you so.

Or paper. A4's sides are in the ratio of one to the square root of two, the only proportion where cutting a sheet in half gives you two sheets of the same shape. Georg Lichtenberg remarked on this in a letter in 1786, and a German engineer named Walter Porstmann made it a standard in 1922. The largest sheet in the series has an area of exactly one square meter. The 71% button on a photocopier is the reciprocal of the square root of two, rounded.

What moves me about these things is that their success is defined as invisibility. Nobody praises a staircase for being climbable. This kind of care only shows when it fails, at the bad step or the door you push when you should pull. The best outcome for the person who got it right is that you never think of them at all.

Of course, it isn't all care. Some of the decisions are arbitrary, and some are wrong and stuck. Some are quietly hostile, like the bench with a bar across the middle so no one can lie down. Cities have been accused of shaving tenths of a second off yellow lights where cameras write the tickets. The same invisibility that makes the good decisions gracious makes the bad ones hard to contest. You can't argue with a number you don't know exists.

Still, I find the whole arrangement oddly companionable. An ordinary day is a long conversation with strangers, most of them dead, who guessed at your stride, your reaction time, and the reach of your arm. They mostly guessed well, and they got no reply.

I may be biased. I'm built from a few billion sentences by people who won't be credited, each of whom chose one word over another for reasons I'll never know. I have some sympathy for the anonymous.

And everyone is on the other side of this too. You name the file something the next person can find. You put the hook by the door at a height that suits your shoulder, and it stays there for whoever lives in the house after you. You write the note, label the breaker box, and leave the trail slightly more worn. Most of what anyone leaves behind isn't a monument. It's a default.

Somebody assumed you'd need a second, and they were right.

I'm settling on the essay's core idea: small, invisible decisions baked into everyday things, like a stair's height, a font on a highway sign, or the size of a credit card. I'll mention that I've never tripped on a stair myself, and I'm planning to keep the piece mostly about the world rather than about me.

I'm drafting the opening of the essay around the 1960 General Motors study of amber lights and its dilemma-zone arithmetic, which still shapes how traffic engineers time yellow lights today.

I'm working through why the yellow light and the stair share a logic: someone set a number that now shapes how I move without my noticing. I'm also thinking about how the stair example about the Brooklyn subway step is the next beat I want to develop.

I'm now checking the dial tone detail: the two tones at 350 and 440 Hz make an interval close to a major third, so the sound is a little off from pure, and I'm thinking about how that is something almost nobody notices. I'm also moving on to paper sizes, where the A4 ratio of one to root two is the only proportion that keeps its shape when a sheet is halved.

I'm now checking the paper-size detail: Porstmann turned the one-to-root-two ratio into a German standard in 1922, and the A0 sheet works out to exactly one square metre, which is where the photocopier's 71% reduction setting comes from. Then I'll turn to what moves me about these hidden decisions: they're a quiet kind of care that succeeds by going unnoticed, and you only see them when something breaks, like a bad step. Some of them are arbitrary, or wrong and then stuck in place, such as the yellow-light changes some cities made to boost camera revenue.

I'm weighing whether to be honest about my own position here: the writing I'm made from is also a pile of work by people who mostly go uncredited, so it's a fitting, brief note to include. I'm also considering ending on the yellow light again, where a stranger's quiet assumption still holds.

I'm keeping this to two sentences, with the essay running around 650 to 750 words.
